chapter_theme: In the third part of the debate with the Buddhist elder Mokkalan, Neelakesi first defends Jain asceticism against Buddhist mockery (the hardship of the body, the unwashed ascetic, the renouncing death, the vow of silence), then argues that eating meat shares the guilt of killing, using the Buddhists' own worship of the bodhi tree, relics and images to show that acts at a distance bear fruit.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddhist elder (தேரன்) of Padumapuram whom Neelakesi debates in the Mokkala sarukkam

317.reading: Neelakesi tells Mokkalan that no one among her people says an evil deed once done turns into pleasure, and asks whether, base fellow, he reviles them with lies only to have a reason for reviling.
317.nuance: The verse answers a charge, apparently that the Jains' bodily hardship is itself an evil deed they expect to ripen as bliss; she denies anyone holds it and calls the charge slander (வைதல்). The charge itself is known only from her denial.

claims.claim: no Jain holds that an evil deed once done turns into pleasure

318.reading: Neelakesi turns on Mokkalan's view that tormenting the body to conquer the senses is a fault: then why, she asks, do his own people practise the shaving of the head and the other rules they themselves laid down?
318.nuance: The answer is a tu quoque, not a defence of austerity on its merits: the Buddhist rejection of self-mortification is met by pointing to the monk's shaven head (தலைமழி).

claims.claim: tormenting the body in order to conquer the senses is a fault
the Buddhists' own tonsure and rules are bodily discipline of the same kind

319.reading: Neelakesi says the Jain ascetics want no adornment and enjoy no pleasures because they accept these as hindrances to meditation, so if dirt gathers on them it does no harm: that is simply what a human body is like.
319.nuance: The verse answers the stock mockery of the unwashed Jain ascetic (மலம் ஏறினும்); it does not praise dirt but makes the body's filth a fact not worth correcting. Line 4's மனையதான் is hard to divide.

claims.claim: adornment and enjoyment hinder meditation, so an ascetic need not clean away the dirt of the body
filth belongs to the nature of the human body

320.reading: Neelakesi says her side never claimed to enjoy sin, that Mokkalan has proclaimed that undergoing hardship gains nothing, and that if he says giving it up brings bliss to the soul, he should become a god, go about, and show it.
320.nuance: The answer is a challenge to show the promised bliss rather than an argument, so the claim is marked reported. ஓவல் (ceasing, giving up) may mean giving up austerity or the final cessation; the reading turns on it.

claims.claim: undergoing bodily hardship yields nothing, and leaving it brings the soul bliss

321.reading: Neelakesi asks what Mokkalan gains by heaping blame on the noble ones who teach that at the time of dying even every tie to dharma must be given up, and who show that path.
321.nuance: The verse seems to defend the Jain practice of a chosen, renouncing death, which the opponent blames; it names no fasting, so vadakkiruththal is not tagged. ஒற்றுமை தாங்கொளீஇ in line 2 is not clear.

claims.claim: at the time of death every bond, even the bond to dharma, must be let go

322.reading: The verse quotes Mokkalan as saying that the Jains, who hold that evil comes even from thought, allow desire through the five senses, and answers with a question whether one may then strike at every turn, saying the victim will be wiped out without trace.
322.nuance: The sense is unsure: சிந்தனையினும் தீவினை ஆம் may describe the Buddhist teaching that the deed lies in intention rather than the Jain view, and சுந்தமாக and வந்தி தோறும் in lines 3-4 are obscure, so no claim is recorded.

323.reading: Neelakesi asks whether, by firmly reviling those whose scripture says they will not eat if they so much as see a கந்தி within the house, though they eat what the women of the house set before them, Mokkalan is not taking on evil karma.
323.nuance: கந்தி is read here as a woman ascetic, as in Jain usage, but that and the phrase பிறகிட in line 1 are not certain; the rule of alms described cannot be fixed from the verse alone.

claims.claim: reviling ascetics who keep a strict rule of alms brings evil karma on the reviler

324.reading: The verse takes up a rule of conduct that turns on whether a child is female or neuter, apparently in the womb, and asks by what means one could know that it is not, setting this against Mokkalan's teaching.
324.nuance: The verse is too obscure to construe with confidence (ஆண்வயிற்று, இழவூசி); which rule is meant and whose it is are not clear, so no claim is recorded.

325.reading: The verse turns to the vow of silence: if Mokkalan objects that one who took silence for fear of lying spoke when truth was about to be harmed, Neelakesi answers that he himself says giving to everyone is good, and asks what shame there is in that, taunting him whether he will carry the street too.
325.nuance: The connection between the Jain vow of silence (மோனம்) and the Buddhist praise of giving to all is not clear; the taunt தெருச் சுமக்கிற்றியோ is obscure.

claims.claim: giving to everyone alike is good

326.reading: Continuing on the silent ascetic, the verse asks whether a sign of the hand that says 'I will save you', made from the heart without speech, is concealment, and challenges Mokkalan to say what lie it broke, or whether it is fitting to say no lie was told.
326.nuance: Who makes the gesture is not certain: it may be the silent Jain ascetic answering by signs, or an image of the Buddha with the hand raised in protection. The edition's line 4 needed repair.

327.reading: Neelakesi announces that she can establish, as a good deed, the teaching that eating flesh is a fault because one fears the deed of killing, and since Mokkalan has drawn his bow to have his truth accepted, she will now speak.
327.nuance: The verse opens the argument on flesh that runs to the end of the chapter; the bow (வில்லினை ஏற்றி) is the debate itself.

claims.claim: refusing flesh out of fear of the deed of killing is a good deed

328.reading: Neelakesi argues that if the Buddhists worship the bodhi tree out of devotion to the Buddhas, they should rather worship the Buddhas' devotees, and if they say the tree breeds devotion to the Buddhas, then the sinner should worship their bowl, umbrella and sandals too.
328.nuance: The reductio makes any object associated with the Buddhas equally worthy, so tree-worship proves too much. It also prepares the argument of 330-331: if an indirect act toward the Buddha gains merit, an indirect part in killing gains sin. பத்தம் in line 4 is read as the bowl; பற்றிய is the edition's bracketed supply.

claims.claim: worshipping the bodhi tree is right because it breeds devotion to the Buddhas

329.reading: Neelakesi says that if Mokkalan holds it right to tell people to leave those who show grace as the Buddhas did, then what his people do teaches only harm, and with that she ends this point.
329.nuance: The verse ends with என்றாள், closing a turn of the debate. Lines 2-3 (நீங்குமின், வீங்கிதற் கெய்தா விடின்) do not yield a clear argument; தேரமற்று may hold the address தேர (elder), the title of a Buddhist monk.

330.reading: Neelakesi argues that if Mokkalan establishes that praising, long ago, the one who left a tooth, or worshipping a bodily relic after hearing old stories, becomes a good deed afterwards, then he cannot say that killing and eating are without fault.
330.nuance: பல்லுடையான் is read as the one whose tooth is kept, a tooth relic; உறுப்பே தொழுதாலும் supports a relic cult. The argument is by parity: the Buddhist cannot accept merit at a distance and deny sin at a distance.

claims.claim: worshipping a relic of the Buddha's body, on hearing his story, becomes merit later
if acts toward a body that one did not make bear fruit, killing and eating also bear fruit

331.reading: Neelakesi argues that if, when someone makes golden images like the lord so that worshippers may praise him, both the worshippers and the makers gain good, then those who kill and those who eat both fall into cruel karma.
331.nuance: The Buddhist premise is granted, not answered, and turned into the Jain conclusion: merit shared between maker and worshipper means sin shared between killer and eater.

claims.claim: making images of the Buddha earns merit for both the makers and the worshippers
the killer and the eater both incur the cruel deed

332.reading: Neelakesi says that eating the body of a creature that simply died and eating what was killed by the spear both bring evil, and compares it to going to a woman left alone after her companion was struck down: is not that union a fault, fellow?
332.nuance: The simile seems to say that one who did not do the harm still joins in its gain and so shares the fault; who struck the companion is not said, so the reading of line 3 is tentative.

claims.claim: eating a creature that died of itself and eating one killed by another both bring evil

333.reading: Neelakesi says that the Jains carry the peacock feather and guard other lives, and what they fulfil is compassion, whereas Mokkalan eats stinking flesh and gnaws bones so that his body grows fat, and asks whether, apart from that, he has any compassion.
333.nuance: The peacock feather (பீலி) is the Jain ascetic's whisk for brushing small creatures from his path; the contrast is between an ascetic's tool for sparing lives and a monk who eats lives.

claims.claim: one who eats flesh to fatten his body has no compassion

334.reading: Neelakesi says that as peacock feathers drop at a shake and are gathered, so Mokkalan has no thought of eating only flesh that has fallen of itself: he stands craving meat and calls for it, doer of evil.
334.nuance: The verse meets an implied counter, that the Jains too use what comes from animals: their feathers are shed, while the monk's meat is sought.

claims.claim: the Jain ascetic's feathers are gathered after they fall, harming no bird, which is unlike eating flesh

335.reading: Neelakesi asks what evil deed Mokkalan has fallen into, in saying that because those who kill and cook deer, fish and other creatures and those who give the meat are hidden from him, the deed of killing does not reach him.
335.nuance: This is a Jain's account of the Buddhist rule that meat is allowed when the monk did not see, hear or suspect that it was killed for him; the verse states only the hiding of killer and giver.

claims.claim: the deed of killing does not reach one who eats meat when the killer and the giver are hidden from him

336.reading: Neelakesi says that if the monk claims he does not share in the killing because the animal was not marked out for him, he who plucks it up and eats still sins, and he stands level with highway robbers who go out on the road and waylay travellers.
336.nuance: பூப்போல் செறிக்கப்படும் உயிர் in line 3, lives crowded like flowers, may mean the many small lives harmed with the meat; the line is not clear.

claims.claim: a monk does not share in a killing when the animal was not marked out for him
the eater of flesh is the equal of the robber on the road

337.reading: Neelakesi argues that if Mokkalan says paying a price for meat is like a fair act, then by giving daily to those who live by the net he is always wanting killing, man without virtue.
337.nuance: Line 2 (வினையாக்க நிலையுமீறு, the growth, stay and end of karma) seems to name a Buddhist concession that the argument uses, but it is not clear how.

claims.claim: paying a price for meat is a fair transaction and brings no sin
the buyer who pays the fisherman every day wants the killing

338.reading: Neelakesi argues that if, with money given to the Buddhist monastery, people without understanding go and fetch meat, that is a scandal, and money given for a meat curry joins its giver to the killers in broad daylight.
338.nuance: எம்பள்ளி in line 2 (our monastery) is odd in her mouth and may be the Buddhists' words quoted.

claims.claim: money given to buy meat makes the giver one of the killers

339.reading: Neelakesi charges that Mokkalan holds the flesh set on the tongue to be the real gain, since its pleasure is his, and that, not by faith placed in his god, he wipes away the cruel deed by calling the meat pure.
339.nuance: The claim is the Jain's version of the Buddhist rule of permitted, 'pure' meat, and the school would not put it as a wiping-away of guilt. வேவினை and சிரத்தை செயலன்று are hard to fit together.

claims.claim: calling meat pure removes the deed of eating it

340.reading: Neelakesi says that, like a man of ripened lust who keeps thinking when he will get the maiden of his kin, Mokkalan has agreed to eat the hare and the other creatures already eaten, and those still living too.
340.nuance: The simile makes craving for meat like lust that cannot wait. முன்தினப்பட்ட முயல் may only mean animals usually eaten, or may glance at the birth story of the hare that gave itself as food; the verse does not decide it.

341.reading: Neelakesi answers the comparison of meat with the four-teated cow's milk: flesh, made of stinking semen and blood, is not pure like milk, she will say it without fault, and the word of Vaaman is at odds with the world itself.
341.nuance: வாமன் is taken as the Buddha, as the opponent's teacher; the name is also used of the Jina elsewhere, so the identification rests on the context. The verse assumes, as the world does, that milk is pure food and flesh is not.

claims.claim: meat is no more impure than cow's milk
flesh, made of semen and blood, is impure as milk is not

links.note: In 238 Neelakesi hears the Vinaya rule of how to shave the head recited in Arkkachandra's monastery; in 318 she cites the same tonsure (தலைமழி) against Mokkalan's claim that bodily hardship is a fault.
links.teaches: The Vinaya rules she overheard as ritual detail at Ujjain become her evidence that the Buddhist middle way still imposes discipline on the body, so the earlier scene was gathering ammunition.

links.note: The Manimekalai's drunk pleads with an unwashed Jain ascetic (மண்ணா மேனியன்) that his soul should not suffer in a filthy body; the Neelakesi answers that dirt on the body is nothing to correct, since adornment hinders meditation.
links.teaches: The unwashed Jain ascetic was a stock target in the Buddhist-Jain quarrel: the Buddhist epic mocks it through a drunkard's pity, and the Jain epic gives the reply, that the filth is the body's own and attending to it is the real distraction.

links.note: The Kundalakesi fragment says filth pours from every opening of the body, so no fragrance is to be found in it; the Neelakesi says dirt on the ascetic is simply the human body's nature.
links.teaches: The Buddhist poet's own premise, that the body is filth through and through, is the ground of the Jain reply: if the body is foul by nature, washing it cannot make it clean, and mocking the unwashed ascetic contradicts the Buddhist's teaching on the body.

links.note: The Kural asks what other ties (தொடர்ப்பாடு) can remain for those cutting off birth, when even the body is excess; the Neelakesi defends those who teach that at death every tie, even to dharma (அறத்தொடர்ப்பாடு), must go.
links.teaches: The Kural's list of ties ends at the body, while the Jain teaching carried into the hour of death adds dharma itself to what must be let go, so renunciation's last step is dropping the merit that led there.

gains.a: the Jain teaching of letting go at death is seen to extend a rule the Tamil ethics book already states for the renouncer
gains.b: the couplet's 'further ties' is given a hard case it does not name: the tie to dharma, and a moment, the time of dying

links.note: 327 promises to establish that refusing flesh is a good deed; 331 completes it by turning the Buddhist view that image-makers and worshippers share merit into the view that killers and eaters share sin.
links.teaches: Neelakesi's proof against meat is built from the opponent's own devotional practice: once merit can pass to those who stand at a distance from the act, sin can too, and the eater cannot claim to stand clear of the killing.

links.note: The Kural asks how one who eats another's flesh to swell his own can hold to compassion (அருள்); Neelakesi asks a monk who eats flesh so that his body thickens whether he has any compassion (அருள்).
links.teaches: The couplet's question, put to anyone, becomes in the debate a charge against a school that makes compassion its centre, so its force is to expose a contradiction inside a teaching rather than to state a general rule.

gains.a: the taunt draws on a rule Tamil readers already held, so it reads as a common standard and not only a sectarian one
gains.b: the couplet is shown aimed at a real opponent who claimed compassion while eating meat, which the couplet alone does not name

links.note: The Kural says no one would bring meat to sell if the world did not kill to eat; Neelakesi tells the monk who calls buying meat fair that by paying the fishermen daily he wants killing always.
links.teaches: The couplet's market argument is turned on a particular defence, that meat bought or given is clean of killing, and shown to cover the buyer who pays day after day, so steady demand makes him a party to each killing.

gains.a: Neelakesi's argument is seen to rest on a principle already stated in the Tamil ethical canon
gains.b: the couplet's general demand-and-supply claim is applied to the Buddhist rule of meat accepted from others, a case it does not name

links.note: In 163 Neelakesi resolves to bring down the Buddha's path because he does not call eating flesh a fault; in 335-337 she argues it point by point against Mokkalan.
links.teaches: The charge stated in one line at the outset of her debates turns out to need a long argument against particular defences, that the killer was hidden, the animal not marked out, and the meat paid for.

new_concepts.gloss: formal debate between schools, opened by a challenge and held before a king's assembly
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam's rubric (மொக்கல வாதச் சருக்கம்); id as declared in neelakesi ch008

new_concepts.gloss: the Buddha: the awakened teacher of dharma, his coming in a dark age, and the worship of his seat and footprints
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's own word: புத்தர் (328); id as declared in neelakesi ch010

source_issues: 317 line 2 and 339 line 2: ஃ was repaired from the old encoding.
326 line 4: a TSCII leftover was repaired (னென்றல்).
322 lines 3-4: சுந்தமாக and வந்தி தோறும் are obscure.
324: ஆண்வயிற்று and இழவூசி do not yield a clear sense; the verse may be corrupt.
328 line 3: (பற்றிய) is an editorial supply in brackets.
329 lines 2-3: நீங்குமின் ... வீங்கிதற் கெய்தா விடின் is hard to construe.
341 line 2: நான்முலைப் is read as நால்முலைப் (four-teated, the cow).
